item.title: Apple's iCloud outage traced to an internal update, not a cyberattack
item.description:
Apple suffered a widespread service outage on Tuesday, with iCloud sign-ins, iCloud Mail, the App Store, Apple Business, AppleCare on Device, and some school services all affected from around 11:45 a.m. ET. Users reported being unable to sign in to their Apple Accounts, sync Photos and Notes, or complete purchases in Apple retail stores. Apple's System Status page listed eight issues, three of them full outages.

Apple later told Bloomberg the problems were caused by an unspecified "internal update" and were not a cyberattack, and that most systems had been restored. It's a reminder of how much of the Apple ecosystem depends on a single sign-in: when Apple Accounts falter, everything from device setup to in-store checkout goes with them.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple’s Cloud Services Are Having a Bad Day, Including Their Status Page

item.title: Memory shortage could keep prices high through 2030 as Apple locks in Samsung supply
item.description:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping component prices — and potentially device prices — elevated. Apple is reportedly one of 14 customers that have locked in priority orders, but those contracts do not protect against market-driven price increases, and Apple is said to be close to signing a similar long-term DRAM deal with Samsung.

Apple had ridden out the global chip shortage for some time on existing orders, but by February 2026 it was reportedly paying double its previous DRAM rate. For buyers, the upshot is that the era of falling memory prices — and the device discounts that came with it — looks over for the foreseeable future.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]
  • AppleInsider News: Chip shortage forces Apple to sign long-term contract with Samsung

item.title: Apple accused of silencing iPhone Duo supplier over display cracks
item.description:
Apple allegedly pressured component supplier Fine M-Tec to withdraw a public statement distancing itself from the display-cracking issue affecting some iPhone Duo units, according to The Elec. The Korean supplier, which makes internal metal plates supporting the foldable screen, had posted a statement last month denying that defects in its components were responsible for the failures, shortly before Apple itself acknowledged the problem.

The number of cracked screens appears small, but the allegation matters less for the scale of the defect than for what it suggests about Apple's handling of it: a supplier publicly pushing back on blame is unusual in Apple's orbit. Meanwhile, Apple has begun selling iPhone Duo replacement parts through its Self Service Repair store, and shipping estimates for new orders have improved to December 17–28, in time for the holidays.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Accused of Silencing iPhone Duo Supplier Over 'Crackgate' Issue

item.title: Siri AI gets daily usage limits in 2027, with iCloud+ perks — except in the UK
item.description:
Apple has begun detailing how Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features that rely on powerful server models will be capped by daily usage limits from the 2027 software releases. The features remain free for users with a supported device, but heavy users will hit a daily cap unless they have increased access — which Apple says will be included with most iCloud+ plans at no additional cost in most countries.

The notable exception is the UK, where Apple says the increased access will not be available with iCloud+ plans, leaving UK users with no clear workaround for now. The limits arrive with iOS 27.3 next month, which also brings a redesigned Apple Health app. The move mirrors rivals that meter server-based AI; the UK carve-out will likely draw questions about a paid tier there.

item.title: 178 major websites compromised in attack targeting iPhone users
item.description:
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, a third-party platform companies use to test and customize their websites, to inject malicious JavaScript into the sites of 178 organizations — including the BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, Zoom, and Salesforce. The code was designed to steal cryptocurrency and credit card data, with one vector aimed at iPhones and iPads on older iOS versions.

Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far only a few thousand dollars appear to have been stolen. But the scale is striking: ordinary visitors to hugely popular sites were exposed without clicking anything suspicious. It's a reminder that the weakest link is often a third-party script a trusted site loads — and that keeping iOS updated is the simplest defense.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Major websites compromised to steal crypto from iPhone users
  • AppleInsider News: iPhone, iPad targeted by massive website malware attack
  • MacRumors: iPhone Users Targeted in Major Website Security Breach

item.title: iPhone set to gain share in 2027 as the smartphone market shrinks
item.description:
Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year to roughly 270 million units, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a Morgan Stanley research report published November 16. That stands out against a bleak industry backdrop: worldwide shipments are expected to fall 5% to 1.04 billion units in 2027, following an estimated 13.8% contraction in 2026, driven by economic pressures and surging memory prices.

The forecast is a substantial downgrade from Morgan Stanley's previous expectation of 3.6% industry growth, yet Apple is expected to grow through the downturn — a sign of how its premium positioning and installed base insulate it from the price pressures hitting Android makers hardest. If it holds, Apple emerges from the slump with its largest-ever share of a shrinking market.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump
  • AppleInsider News: iPhone relatively safe while the rest of the smartphone market contracts

item.title: Google Wallet comes to iPhone — but without tap to pay
item.description:
Google Wallet is now available on iPhone in the United States, giving users a way to organize payment cards, tickets, boarding passes, and receipts in one place, with package tracking synced from Gmail and other Google apps. Users can also scan loyalty and membership cards with the camera to import them.

The catch is at the checkout counter: Google Wallet cannot be used for tap-to-pay purchases in stores, so Apple Pay remains the only option for contactless payments on iPhone. The app does work for online checkout anywhere Google Pay is accepted. It's a useful organizer for people deep in Google's ecosystem, but as a wallet replacement it stops well short — a limitation that reflects Apple's continued control over NFC payments on its devices.

item.title: HomeView teardown finds a device that's nearly impossible to repair
item.description:
iFixit's teardown of Apple's new HomeView smart home hub found a device that takes a step backward in repairability compared to the HomePod. Strong adhesive holds the display in place and was difficult to remove, opening the device damaged internal components, and a mix of Phillips and Torx screws in different sizes means several tools are needed to get inside. Speakers take up most of the space behind the display.

The teardown also revealed the differences between the two models: the wall-mounted version gets smaller speakers than the speaker-base model. For a device meant to sit on a wall or counter for years, the poor repairability is a notable blemish on Apple's first smart home hub — even as regulators push Apple on repair access.

item.title: iPhone Duo gets face unlock in iOS 27.3 beta 2
item.description:
Apple seeded the second developer beta of iOS 27.3, and its headline feature answers the most common complaint about the iPhone Duo: the foldable finally gets a face-based unlock. A new “Unlock with Front Camera” option lets you open the closed Duo by looking at its outer camera, and hands-on testing found it works well. But it is deliberately not Face ID — a less secure, convenience-only unlock that still requires Touch ID or a passcode for Apple Pay, passwords, and other sensitive actions.

The feature only works on the Lock Screen while the Duo is closed, requires a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, and asks for Touch ID again after about 45 minutes of inactivity. The update is expected to reach the public before the end of the year.

item.title: Siri AI and Apple Intelligence get daily usage limits tied to iCloud+
item.description:
The other big reveal in the 27.3 betas is how Apple plans to charge for heavy AI use. Every device gets a free daily allowance for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side processing — multi-step requests with personal context, Image Playground, and Clean Up in Photos. Once that allowance is used up, users can extend it with an iCloud+ plan.

Apple says simple requests, like sending a text, will always work for free. What remains vague is exactly how large the free daily allowance is. The model puts Apple in line with the rest of the AI industry, where heavy server-side use is metered — but it also means the most capable Siri features could effectively become a subscription perk for power users.

item.title: macOS 27.3 splits Full Disk Access into stricter, clearer permissions
item.description:
macOS 27.3 beta 2 delivers the privacy overhaul Apple promised a month ago, aimed squarely at AI automation apps that ask for sweeping access to your Mac. The old “Device Control and Data Access” toggle is split into two settings — “System & App Protection Override” and Accessibility — so it is clearer what an app is actually being allowed to do, and granting the highest level of access now requires much more explicit user action.

The change matters because apps with Full Disk Access can read email, edit contacts and photos, monitor keystrokes, track websites, and record the screen. Apple’s concern is that too many users were granting that level of access without grasping what it entailed — a notable counterweight to the AI-agent trend, as more apps want to act on your behalf.

item.title: iPhone Duo momentum: 200,000 optimized apps and pre-Christmas delivery
item.description:
Two signs the iPhone Duo launch is going better than expected landed on the same day. Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the foldable — double the 100,000 figure from just ten days earlier. These are apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later that fill the Duo’s inner and outer displays properly.

At the same time, supply has improved enough that new U.S. orders placed today are estimated to arrive December 16–23, a full month earlier than the January 25 estimate in place as recently as last Thursday. And the Duo got a celebrity boost: Oprah Winfrey surprised 120 caregivers in her live “Favorite Things” audience with the $1,999 foldable — a high-profile endorsement just weeks after launch.

item.title: More in 27.3 beta 2: Siri reads whole webpages, answers health questions, and video podcasts come to TV
item.description:
Beyond the headliners, beta 2 is packed with smaller additions. Siri AI gains an “Ask About Page” feature in Safari that can read an entire webpage — including content below the fold — so you can ask it to find gluten-free options on a long menu or build a packing list from a travel guide. Siri can also now answer questions about your Health app data, closing a gap where the older Siri Classic could do this but Siri AI’s guardrails blocked it.

The Apple TV app gains video podcasts, free to watch without an Apple TV+ subscription. Apple News+ Puzzles expand to subscribers in the UK, Australia, and French Canada. And Apple Intelligence in China, which arrived on iPhone in beta 1, now extends to iPad and Mac.

item.title: Apple Pay chief retires as leadership overhaul continues
item.description:
Apple’s ongoing leadership reshuffle reached Apple Pay. Jennifer Bailey, vice president of Internet Services and Apple Pay, is retiring after 23 years at the company, and Bloomberg reports her successor will be Corey Fugman, an Apple lifer who joined 26 years ago. Apple has not commented on the report, and it is not yet clear whether Fugman takes on all of Bailey’s responsibilities.

Separately, Arthur Levinson — former chairman and current lead independent director — filed with the SEC to sell 90,000 shares worth about $31.8 million. Such planned sales by senior figures are routine, but coming on the same day as the Apple Pay transition, it adds to a picture of a company in the middle of a generational changing of the guard.

item.title: Apple reportedly has 18 new products lined up for 2027
item.description:
With the iPhone Duo, HomeView, and PROLED MacBook Pro launches behind it, Apple’s 2027 slate is already taking shape — and it is expected to be big. MacRumors counts at least 18 new products next year, headlined by the 20th-anniversary iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max, all-new smart glasses, a larger HomeView, and AirPods Pro with cameras.

Early rumors about the anniversary iPhone suggest it will borrow heavily from the iPhone Air, with a more rounded all-glass design and a new main camera sensor built on a faster 17nm imaging process. The reports are still early and partly from leakers with mixed track records — but the scale of the lineup points to 2027 being another unusually busy year for Apple hardware.

item.title: Some PROLED MacBook Pro owners report eye strain and dizziness
item.description:
Some owners of the new MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with a significant number of complaints appearing on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the models launched earlier this month. Affected users point to the screen’s brightness-control system as a possible explanation.

It is too early to say how widespread the issue is — reports so far are anecdotal, and OLED displays have drawn similar complaints from sensitive users on phones and other devices for years. But with the PROLED screen being the star feature of the new MacBook Pro, Apple will be watching whether this stays limited to a small, sensitive minority.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness

item.title: Apple's Siri-powered smart glasses reportedly coming at WWDC 2027
item.description:
Apple's first smart glasses are reportedly on track for a WWDC 2027 unveiling, with shipping before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The glasses, internally code-named N50, are said to be slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans, with oval camera openings integrated into the frame and a front light indicating use or charging. They will not offer Vision Pro-style augmented reality; instead, the pitch is Siri AI plus deep integration with iPhone apps, in a similar spirit to CarPlay and HomeView.

The idea is that the glasses lean on the apps and services already on your iPhone, with Siri AI doing the heavy lifting — Gurman says Apple is already asking developers to prepare for a 2027 introduction, and privacy features are expected to be built around the Secure Enclave. Not everyone is convinced the category will survive: The Verge's David Pierce, reacting to Gurman's report, argued there's a real chance the market rejects smart glasses so completely by next June that Apple never ships them.

item.title: iPhone Duo 2 may finally add Face ID, a telephoto camera, and an Action button
item.description:
Apple has four goals for future iPhone Duo models, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman: Face ID, an Action button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter design. Engineers have already built Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID on the outer display, but the feature is reportedly running out of time to be finalized for the late-2027 model, so it may not arrive until the iPhone Duo 3. The Action button would most likely be combined with the camera control button.

Meanwhile, early adopters are finding one rough edge with the current Duo, out about three weeks now: apps not yet updated for iOS 27 get letterboxed, and one suggested fix is a default split-view option that would make unoptimized apps less awkward. Most apps people rely on are already updated for iOS 27, but a fair number of iOS 26-era apps still show the black bars.

item.title: Apple launches research study on AI for health
item.description:
Apple has announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study in the United States, a virtual research study with an associated app exploring how AI can be used for health. The study signals Apple's growing interest in applying AI to health and wellness, an area where the company already collects vast amounts of data through the Apple Watch and iPhone. Details on what the study will measure and how participants can join are in Apple's announcement.

item.title: Apple reiterates its commitment to the visionOS platform
item.description:
This week's Apple Vision Pro newsletter leads with Apple reaffirming that it remains committed to the visionOS platform, alongside a look at how Apple records content on the Vision Pro. The message lands as questions continue about the headset's long-term future, and it suggests Apple is not backing away from its spatial computing bet even as its attention shifts toward lighter wearable devices.

item.title: Slow Horses likely ends after season 8 as it catches up with the books
item.description:
Apple TV+'s Emmy and BAFTA-winning spy drama Slow Horses may not continue past its eighth season, which Apple confirmed back in September. The show is catching up with Mick Herron's book series, and Olivia Cooke — who plays Sid Baker — told The Times she is shooting "the last season," adding "never say never" about whether it could return. For fans, season 8 may be the final run of Gary Oldman's Slough House crew, at least until more books arrive.

Sources

  • AppleInsider: Apple TV+ 'Slow Horses' faces the glue factory after eight seasons

item.title: New Apple TV has double the RAM, but apps still can't use it
item.description:
The new Apple TV 4K packs an A19 chip, 128 GB of storage, and 8 GB of RAM — twice the memory of the previous model, a jump partly tied to the memory chip supply crunch that also helped push the box to a $299 price point. But apps and games can't actually use the extra memory: tvOS still caps each app at 2 GB of RAM, and that limit hasn't changed on the fourth-generation box. The extra RAM may help the system in other ways, but for now it doesn't translate into more headroom for the apps you run.

item.title: HomeView reviews land: great hardware, software still finding itself
item.description:
Apple's new HomeView smart display started shipping this week, and the first reviews agree on a split verdict: the hardware is a pleasure, the software is a work in progress. Jason Snell calls the screen "a pleasure to touch and tilt" and the hardware "solid and coherent," but says the software feels like "a peculiar amalgam" of other Apple products — its main interface resembles an overgrown Apple Watch, some apps feel escaped from iPhone or iPad, others straight off Apple TV. Joanna Stern's video review was equally warm on the experience overall, and both reviewers see real promise underneath the seams.

One detail that stood out across the coverage: HomeView's Ambient Dark Mode, which adapts the display to its surroundings, is good enough that 9to5Mac argues it should come to every Apple device. The consensus is that HomeView is a late arrival with a strong foundation — worth watching as Apple polishes the software, but early buyers should expect some rough edges.

item.title: Could Apple chip chief Johny Srouji jump to Nvidia?
item.description:
Semafor reported that Nvidia is "considering" Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji for a leadership role, and the speculation set off a round of debate among Apple watchers. Author Patrick McGee argued Srouji would be "an incredible choice" for Nvidia and might even accept, saying he has "hit the ceiling at Apple and won't ever be CEO" while remaining ambitious and eager to have chip designs dictate product timelines.

John Gruber pushed back, saying his money is on Srouji having no interest in the job. Nothing is confirmed — this is reporting about Nvidia considering a candidate, not an offer or a departure — but the chatter alone underscores how central Srouji has become to Apple's identity: the architect of Apple silicon is now the kind of executive rival chipmakers covet.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Patrick McGee on Johny Srouji and Nvidia

item.title: Apple rethinks how it builds iOS 28 and macOS 28
item.description:
With the last of the big hardware launches of the fall now behind it, Apple is changing its internal approach to developing iOS 28 and macOS 28. The new process is meant to give engineers more time to explore and develop new features within existing update cycles, rather than racing everything toward a single annual deadline — a shake-up that could mean steadier, better-baked releases.

Meanwhile, developers are continuing to optimize their apps for the iPhone Duo's larger inside display, the all-new form factor that is reshaping how apps lay out and multitask. The week's coverage paints a picture of a company catching its breath after a wild few months and quietly retooling how it ships software.

item.title: Beats 360 vs Studio Pro: which over-ears to buy?
item.description:
Apple's new Beats 360 headphones, launched in September, are the first Beats over-ears since the Studio Pro arrived in 2023 — and the older model is still on sale at a lower price, so the choice isn't obvious. The Beats 360 bring the newer design and the latest features, while the Studio Pro now represents the value play in the lineup.

Which one wins depends on what you value: the 360 if you want the newest hardware and are willing to pay for it, the Studio Pro if you'd rather save money on a still-capable pair. With both models in the mix and holiday deals starting, it's a good moment to compare them side by side before buying.

item.title: Milton turns an old iPad into a HomeView-style dashboard
item.description:
Don't want to buy a HomeView to get a smart-home display? A new indie app called Milton offers a DIY alternative: it turns older iPads running iPadOS 17 or later into a home dashboard, serving a similar purpose to Apple's new display using hardware you already own.

It's a neat fit for the week HomeView launched — a reminder that the idea of a wall- or counter-mounted home hub doesn't have to start with new hardware. If you have an old iPad gathering dust, Milton gives it a second life as the center of your smart home.

item.title: HomeView and new Apple TV 4K launch today
item.description:
Apple's two big home products are officially out today: the all-new HomeView smart display ($299) and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, both announced October 13 and now shipping to pre-order customers and on sale in Apple Stores. HomeView is Apple's first smart home display, powered by Siri AI, with a 7-inch screen that recognizes up to six users by face and gives each a personalized home screen. Apple also published support guides and release notes for HomeView software 27.2, covering facial recognition, multiuser profiles, and repairs — plus the caveat that it may not recognize you in sunglasses.

Early impressions are mixed but enthusiastic: reviewers praise the build quality, sound, and a record-low 0.3-nit minimum brightness that suits a bedside table, while questioning how much it adds to a home already full of Apple devices. Apple executives told TechRadar the design was a "hard fought, fun journey" balancing audio, privacy, and Siri AI. The new Apple TV 4K brings the A19 chip, Siri AI, an updated Siri Remote with Find My, and four-speaker surround support.

item.title: Siri AI reaches older Apple TV 4K models — but not HomePod mini 2
item.description:
Apple released tvOS 27.2.1 today, bringing Siri AI to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models from 2021 and 2022. A paired Siri AI-enabled device nearby is required, since the older boxes can't run it on their own. The update had been conspicuously absent when Apple shipped its other 27.2.1 updates earlier in the week — apparently held back to coincide with the new Apple TV 4K launch.

Meanwhile, the HomePod mini 2 is still waiting: today's HomePod software 27.2.1 does not enable Siri AI on the new speaker, and Apple's site still says only "coming in a future software update" with no timeframe. The mini 2 has just 2GB of RAM, well below the 8GB minimum for on-device Siri AI, so personal-context requests will need a paired Apple Intelligence iPhone or iPad. Some new Apple TV 4K owners hit a YouTube app error; the fix is to install tvOS 27.2, restart, or reinstall the app.

item.title: Epic asks Supreme Court to uphold contempt ruling against Apple
item.description:
Epic Games has filed its formal response to Apple's Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Epic argues Apple complied with the letter of the judge's steering order — allowing developers to link out to alternative payment options — while undermining its spirit with fees and friction that kept the old system effectively intact.

The filing sets up the next chapter of the long-running saga: oral arguments are scheduled for January 11, 2027. The stakes are the App Store's payment rules and the tens of billions in commissions they generate, so the Court's decision could reshape how iOS apps take payments in the US for years to come.

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage nears 24 hours, now resolving
item.description:
A global Microsoft 365 outage that began around 1 p.m. Eastern on Thursday knocked out Outlook email and disrupted Teams, Copilot, and other services for nearly a full day, with almost 130,000 Outlook reports logged on Downdetector shortly after it started. Exchange Online was at the center of it, and Exchange accounts in Apple Mail were affected too.

By Friday evening Microsoft said the underlying issue was fixed and it was seeing "broad recovery and stability" as it restored access. Microsoft blamed failed server health checks, not hackers, and extended email timeouts to 48 hours to preserve delayed mail during the disruption. It hit businesses and government operations, with Japan confirming a significant impact on its government IT systems.

item.title: iPhone Duo survives 450,000 folds — and tops 100,000 apps
item.description:
CNET's three-week hinge stress test of the iPhone Duo has passed 451,000 folds, and the phone still works — though the hinge is showing wear. It started feeling looser around 390,000 folds, and by 440,300 the mechanism had shifted enough that the screen stopped 5 to 10 degrees short of fully open, with the distinctive snap gone. It can still be opened fully by hand.

Apple also says more than 100,000 apps have now been built for the Duo — though many are simple refactors rather than apps fully redesigned for the big foldable display, and developers warn it will take time before favorite apps really take advantage of it.

item.title: iPhone 18 and 18e coming spring 2027 with A20 chip
item.description:
Apple's iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e will launch in spring 2027 with the new A20 chip, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reiterated on the latest episode of his "Power On" podcast, in line with his earlier reporting. The iPhone Air 2 is expected at the same time.

The timing confirms Apple's split launch cadence: the Pro models arrive in the fall, while the standard iPhone 18, the budget 18e, and the Air 2 follow the next spring. That puts the base iPhone 18 roughly six months behind the iPhone 18 Pro, a staggered schedule that would have been unthinkable a few years ago but now looks like Apple's settled rhythm.

item.title: First Apple Home Collection accessories now available to order
item.description:

item.title: Apple meets Thai officials over spyware warnings
item.description:
Apple met with Thai officials earlier this week to discuss spyware warnings sent to politicians and other users in the country, Bloomberg reports. The talks followed Apple's October 29 threat notifications, which reached users in 99 countries after Apple identified activity consistent with mercenary spyware attacks, raising concerns about surveillance of Thai political figures.

Thailand's Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after the meeting that the alerts alone do not establish that attackers actually succeeded in compromising devices. The episode is a reminder that Apple's threat notifications — now sent to users in nearly a hundred countries — are a warning of targeted attack activity, not confirmation of a successful hack.

item.title: HomeView launches tomorrow as reviews land: charming but unfinished
item.description:
Apple's first smart home display, the HomeView, arrives Friday, November 13, with the first pre-orders already reaching customers in Australia and New Zealand. Reviews are warm but measured: The Verge calls it powerful enough to run a smart home, MacStories rounds up praise for a simple, charming device built for Apple users, and 9to5Mac says it earns its place — while AppleInsider sees a shallow launch with incredible potential and Six Colors a late arrival still showing seams.

The launch is already a bit messy. Apple has pushed out a day-zero software update fixing nine security vulnerabilities, and a December update is promised to fix Siri glitches — including Siri once claiming the device has no camera, and refusing to open a garage door or unlock a front door it recognized the owner for. The first Apple Home Collection accessories — LG indoor and outdoor cameras and a video doorbell — go on sale Friday for December delivery. Apple also detailed how Secure Exclaves isolate the HomeView's camera and microphone data from the rest of the system.

item.description:
The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K launches Friday, four years after its predecessor, and reviewers agree on the verdict: it's the best streamer you can buy, at a price that's hard to justify. item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in disgrace; Trump taps Tim Cook, Srouji eyed as successor
item.description:
Nvidia announced that co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned effective immediately, after reports of multiple extramarital affairs — including one with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. The board had initially backed him, but moved after a second affair surfaced and the company's market value fell by more than $800 billion. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement, and Huang has agreed to testify before Congress behind closed doors by Thanksgiving.

The story keeps looping back to Apple. President Trump posted that Tim Cook should be Nvidia's next CEO, calling him the only man for the job. Separately, Semafor reports that Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji — the architect of the move from Intel to Apple silicon — is among the candidates under consideration, though it's unclear whether he has been approached or would be interested.

item.title: Nvidia board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
item.description:
Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust CEO and founder Jensen Huang as soon as Wednesday, after a second extramarital affair came to light. The New York Times reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him — a potential violation of the company's code of conduct. That followed an earlier report that Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence determined is a suspected Chinese spy.

The board has been working with an outside firm to identify CEO candidates and is weighing naming an interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement, with CFO Colette Kress reportedly favored by some directors for the interim role. Directors were set to meet Wednesday to decide Huang's future, and the board has briefed the White House on its planned meeting. Huang's departure would end the era in which he drove the global AI boom and made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.

item.title: Apple abruptly shutters its Support Community forums
item.description:
Apple abruptly placed the Apple Support Community into a read-only state on Tuesday and announced the forums will permanently close on Friday, November 20. Contributors — some of whom volunteered on the site for more than two decades — were blindsided, with no chance to post farewell messages.

Reactions were mixed. Jason Snell called the boards an embarrassment for Apple, outdated and misleadingly official-looking under an apple.com domain, and said good riddance. Others noted the forums, for all their generic point-chasing answers, were sometimes genuinely useful, and that the volunteers deserved a proper goodbye. The forums will remain online as a searchable archive of answers, but no new questions or discussions will be possible.

item.title: Apple employee charged after fatal crash near Apple Park kills toddler
item.description:
Apple employee Eric Chen Su was arrested and charged with suspicion of gross vehicular manslaughter following a fatal collision near the Apple Park Visitor Center on Friday. Shortly after noon, Su was reportedly traveling between 90 and 100 miles per hour when he struck the back of a stopped vehicle occupied by a two-year-old girl and her babysitter. Both were seriously injured and taken to a hospital; the child, Riley Howard, died, while the babysitter survived. Su sustained light injuries.

Apple said in a statement that its hearts are broken, and the incident has shaken the community around its Cupertino campus. The crash occurred at the intersection of North Tantau Avenue and Pruneridge Avenue, right next to the Visitor Center.

item.title: iPhone Duo, one week in: impressive, but not for everyone
item.description:
A week after launch, the first long-term verdicts on Apple's folding iPhone Duo are landing — and they're mixed. Some early buyers have reportedly returned their devices after the novelty wore off, and 9to5Mac is polling readers on whether they kept or returned theirs. item.title: Binance warns iPhone users of unpatched iOS exploit that can steal data from other apps
item.description:
Crypto exchange Binance is warning iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that researchers say remains unpatched and could allow a malicious app to access sensitive data stored by other apps on the device. In a post on X on November 10, Binance flagged the flaw as affecting multiple iOS versions, including iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2.

The warning matters most to crypto holders, since finance apps are prime targets for data theft, but the underlying issue is broader: a malicious app could potentially reach data used by other apps. Details of the exploit itself remain sparse in the reports. Until Apple ships a fix, the practical advice is the usual — only install apps from trusted developers and keep iOS updated when patches arrive.

item.title: Google Gemini arrives on Apple CarPlay

Google announced Wednesday that a dedicated Gemini app is rolling out on Apple CarPlay worldwide in several languages, starting today. Drivers can tap the Gemini icon on the CarPlay display or side rail to start or resume a conversation, with Gemini Live supporting back-and-forth voice chats — including interrupting, changing the subject, or pausing mid-conversation.

Conversations on the iPhone sync to CarPlay, so a chat started at home can continue on the road. Gemini can pull from your Google apps to give a personalized daily brief, catch you up on unread emails, or tell you when your next appointment starts — and help find a restaurant while driving. It's a notable moment: Google's AI assistant now has a first-class seat on Apple's in-car platform.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max tops CNET battery test of 32 smartphones
item.description:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Max placed first overall in CNET's battery comparison of 32 smartphones, with other iPhone models also leading individual tests and matching significantly more expensive devices. CNET ran two tests totaling three hours and 45 minutes: three hours of video streaming over Wi-Fi at maximum brightness, plus 45 minutes mixing video playback, video calls, gaming, and social media. Each phone started at 100 percent charge, and the publication averaged the remaining percentages for its overall rankings.

The result is a strong showing for Apple's battery life across the iPhone 18 lineup — not just the flagship — and a useful data point for anyone weighing an upgrade this holiday season.
